utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Before we continue with the re-examination of the witness, I would like to ask the Defence if they are in a position to respond to the Prosecution's motion for leave to file an amended Rule 65 ter summary for Witness Dusan Janc. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Mr. President, yes, we are in a position to respond to the Prosecution's motion for leave to file an amended Rule 65 ter summary for Witness Dusan Janc. I will try to be brief. Mr. Janc has already testified here on a number of occasions. We all recall him testifying about the maps, DNA analyses for which he complied a report and numerous footage was introduced through him. Now the Prosecution wishes to seek to tender some additional footage which they list in their motion. They also want to tender some intercepts through this witness, which were allegedly intercepted by Croatian operators. I will deal with the second issue first. I will quote a key sentence of paragraph 4 of the Prosecution's motion, in which it is stated: "His testimony concerning Croatian intercepts will have to do -- will be to the effect of their reliability within the context of other relevant and material evidence in the case." First, I'd like to remind you that Witness PW-070 testified. He listened and was shown to those intercepts. We have his testimony on the record. The Defence wishes to suggest that this issue be dealt in written form the best. If they want to tender those documents, which I believe is their intention, they should submit at least a bar table motion which would resolve the whole thing. For an OTP investigator to address the reliability of this document -- these documents within the context of other relevant material in this case is, in our view, inappropriate. We don't believe such materials should be introduced through an investigator. If I understand correctly, Mr. Dusan Janc is an investigator, rather than an expert. If the OTP wish to deal with those intercepts within the context of all other material, although we don't know what material exactly, because we don't know what their intention is with Dusan Janc and what other documents they have, say, VRS, or AB and H documents or some others. In any case, we could deal with that easily in a written form, and it is up to the Chamber to assign weight to the issue of reliability of those intercepts and to drew conclusions about the various aspects that have to do with the intercepts themselves. Therefore, the Defence position is that in this part the Prosecution motion should be rejected. That is to say, the parts which deal with the Croatian intercepts. As regards the footage, there is a number of such documents, such as the visit of Canadian Serbs to General Mladic; next, the meeting of General Mladic with General Rupert Smith of the 25th of July; then the celebration when one of the VRS generals retired. That evidence has already been introduced through another investigator. We will have a number of other witnesses here appearing, especially from the VRS, but perhaps we should, in view of that, think about whether such material should be introduced through them, because they have direct knowledge of those events, as opposed to the investigators. The Defence will not take a definite position. Now whether it should be done through investigators or some other witnesses, we will leave it in your hands, in keeping with the practice so far and the rules that are in application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gajic. Mr. McCloskey what is the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, on the last point, Mr. Janc and the -- and the videos, we're not intending that Mr. Janc will replace General Milovanovic or the people that are seen on some of the videos. But, as you recall, it's important for you to know how we got the videos for their authenticity, when we got them, and for example, remember the now famous the 25th of July video of General Tolimir in Zepa. You'll need to explain why we think that is the 25th of July, and that is based on things that Mr. Janc knows about in the investigation. So like he did before when he testified about the Skorpion video, I think his basic information is for the authentication of these videos that have been around for a long time and we have just waited until you've seen some of the videos, some of them you haven't. But this is a good time now for you to you hear from him about the issues of why we think this is the 25th, where we got this, how we got it. Those are important things that is best seen from the witness and cross-examined, frankly, in open court. It's much better that way, in my view, and I think you have seen this kind of evidence before and it is not prejudicial to anyone. I think the Defence will want to see this as well. It is very important for them, I think, these dates, and when the General is in Zepa. On the issue of the intercepts, I think we have to go back and remember and I think it was Mr. Elderkin that was putting on the Croatian intercept operator, and who laid a very good foundation, I thought, for those intercepts. And Mr. Elderkin and the team had chosen to, instead of offering them as we could have then, to say, Well, we'd like to give you a little bit more about the authenticity of the intercepts. And now I'll go back to Stephanie Frease. We have to go back in our memories even more. Stephanie Frease was an employ of the OTP. She was a, on the Srebrenica team and on the leadership research team. She testified about the authenticity of the BiH intercepts. If you recall, she was able to compare those intercepts to things that happened on video. When the intercept says there's a Serbian flag flying on the church in Srebrenica she was able to find a video of a Serbian flag flying on the church in Srebrenica. Those kinds of things, where she just put material together from the investigation to show you that the intercepts were, indeed, reflecting what the investigation was seeing on the ground. That's the same thing Mr. Janc is doing. In fact, it's much simpler. As far as I recall, he will be showing you some of the other BiH intercepts that were matches for the Croatian intercepts, or something on the ground that's mentioned in the Croatian intercept that we can actually see through documents. So it's simple, it's something that you should see and should be cross-examined. It's not something that is best left to paper with 92 ter or 92 bis, you must be incredibly overwhelmed with paper. This intercept material is important. I think we would like you to see this final small chapter. The main chapter of the intercepts, like Mr. Gajic said, was the witness. But this is the final little chapter of how they connect with the world that was happening at the time. And so that's what this is based on. Again, it is not prejudicial; it's not untimely, and it's something that Mr. Elderkin mentioned a long time ago that would be coming, and it's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have the positions of the parties on the record. Mr. Gajic, you want to add something. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Peter McCloskey has just clarified some things concerning the potential testimony of Mr. Janc. First of all, he was not a witness to those events. He had no direct participation so as to be able to address them appropriately as a witness. First and foremost, he is appearing here as an OTP investigator, somebody providing OTP lawyers with the material that they use in the courtroom. It is our standing position that such investigators put forth appropriate arguments. If an investigator compares an event to an alleged intercept, in essence, it is simply argumentation and we have final briefs and final arguments, closing arguments for that. And the witnesses are here to say what happened in a specific place. If Mr. McCloskey believes that a certain intercept is authentic, he can put questions to the appropriate witness to see whether such an event, indeed, took place and whether an intercept, indeed, took place. If this is done through an investigator, then, I'm sorry, but it is very difficult to cross-examine an OTP investigator, especially if such an investigator is used, as Dusan Janc was in the past, to introduce additional witness statements into evidence. We cannot expect him to provide direct knowledge. He can only testify to what he has read. And, of course, this Defence is entitled to doubt the veracity of such investigators, because they have a vested interest in working for the OTP. Therefore, as regards intercepts, the best way to address it is in written form. We had PW-070, whom I mentioned. He testified about the intercepts, about the way they did it, et cetera. He was cross-examined, and I believe we have sufficient material to draw conclusions about the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I would like to ask you one thing. We have heard a lot of investigators of the Prosecution as witnesses. Some were -- some names were mentioned by Mr. McCloskey just a minute ago. Some others, like the witness who is coming today, is an investigator. Of course, none of the investigators have taken part in the events or were -- eye-witnesses of the events in 1995. But they testified about other things, about the way the investigation was conducted, the chain of chain of custody of some material. What is, in view of you, the difference between the Witness Janc in this respect, to the other witnesses? I just want to understand your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to other witnesses, what is the difference between the testimony of Dusan Janc and other witnesses? Well, the difference is obvious. He is an OTP investigator. He is not a witness to events. It is one thing when an investigator addresses only the manner in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry, Mr. Gajic, I was not comparing Mr. Janc to eye-witnesses, but to investigators we have heard as witnesses. What is the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, basically, none. I don't see any great difference, save in the matter of topics they testified. There are different topics between Mr. Janc, Erin Gallagher and Mr. Blaszczyk, but they all fall within the group of investigators. It is one thing to have an investigator testifying to the methods of something -- how something came in the possession of the investigators, and perhaps it may be the only investigator who can tell us about that. But I don't believe it is fully appropriate that an investigator should address the issue of authenticity of material by way of comparing it to some other material and other evidence put forth in this case. That was the point of what I was trying to say. We have already had occasion to see that investigators are used to introduce a large amount of evidence, including a number of witness statements who will not appear in this courtroom. And this creates certain problems. The Defence will take a position on that, and I believe we have already stated what our position is on any evidence provided by investigators. Such evidence cannot serve as the basis, the underlying basis, for the judgement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and briefly. We need to remember Stephanie Frease is what -- is basically what -- Janc is taking over her position. She's now in another life. She was a super-investigator as you will, because she was an expert analyst and speaks the language. She testified, I don't believe there was an objection to her. I may be wrong about that. That was a long time ago. But Mr. Janc is -- as will -- will be doing basically what Ms. Frease was doing, it shouldn't be very controversial, but it should help the Court test those intercepts and it will show the Court that the Prosecution has done that, that we're just not taking this on face value, and I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have the positions of both parties heard and on the record, and the Chamber will consider the situation and will come back to you in due course. Another matter, translations of exhibits of the Defence. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to inform the Chamber that the following translations have arrived. D38; D94; D111; D123; D135; and D136. They have been uploaded in e-court and made available to everyone. I believe they should finally be tendered as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, on the same topic actually. As you recall yesterday when the Defence tendered Defence 183 and 184, they didn't have translations. I now have 65 ter 7256, which is identical to 184, and 7255, which is identical to 183, and those 65 ter numbers do have translation. That was our oversight. Somehow these documents had two ERNs, one had a translation and one didn't, and unfortunately the ones we gave to the Defence did not have translations. So they did not have them when they used them yesterday. But those 65 ter numbers do have translations now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what is your position in relation to admission of these documents? The first -- the D183 was only pending -- MFI'd pending translation. The other one was MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's an interesting question because, as you could tell from my comments yesterday, it's -- the Prosecution's been studying the authenticity of these materials, and I was -- and they're so closely related to the Main Staff that when the Defence said they trusted their authenticity, that meant a fair amount to me in this context, which is why I brought out the other document. And I think if we could discuss that other document now, the one that was on the screen that you were talking to me about, that in -- it would help us deal with all three of these. Perhaps together or -- or perhaps differently. But I think this last one is sort of the last piece of the puzzle and I did mention to Mr. Gajic that, as I had with the previous two, I would be asking for his position on this 12 July Popovic document, which is MFI'd as P2069, the one that you were mentioning yesterday, that -- that it didn't have the connections with the witness that you were -- that, according to the rules. And if we could discuss that briefly then I think we can deal with all of them at once. So my first question to the Defence is, if we could put that up on the screen, so it's P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you going to use it with the witness again during your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know, I don't think so. I think I've pretty much finished with it. I just wanted to get the position of the Defence, and then decide whether or not I continued to offer it. Especially based on your comments and also my concerns. But crucial to this process is -- is how the Defence feels or -- or doesn't feel. Of course, they don't have to take a position. But this document is -- is sent from the Drina Corps to the Main Staff, sector for intelligence and affairs, as well as the command of the Drina Corps security. So their position, I would be very interested to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Firstly, we can state that the Defence documents which have now a translation and the numbers were given by Mr. Gajic are now in evidence and no longer MFI'd. Mr. Gajic, what is your position in relation to P2069, MFI?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first, I'd like to address the previous two documents, where we have Momir Nikolic's name in the signature block. Regarding those documents, we said that currently we have no reason to believe that the documents are inauthentic. So the formulation is somewhat different than the one suggested by Mr. McCloskey. As regards this document, I believe it will be best to ask Mr. Nikolic about the authenticity of this document, once he comes here to testify. And then this would apply to the previous two as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is a change from yesterday. My recollection is they felt that the documents were authentic. I don't think you can offer a document on the basis that you don't have evidence that it is not authentic. I think an officer of the court has to have a positive reason to believe it is authentic. And I think did he that yesterday, and that's why you don't find me objecting to these documents. That is, I think, a morph, which we lawyers do sometimes, but I don't think a document can go into evidence on that. There's no evidence that it's a forgery, or there's no evidence that it is not authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I only briefly touched upon the interpretation provided by Mr. McCloskey. We, of course, stand by what we said yesterday. Any document we receive from the OTP for which we believe is authentic will be made use of. As regards the way of how this document was procured, that is something we are ignorant of. We received it from the OTP and from another source which also supplied the OTP. We have no reason to believe something to be inauthentic, unless we have a basis for that. Regarding the two documents of yesterday, for the time being, we hold them to be authentic. It would be crazy if we acted on the basis of some information, such as whether it tallies with this or that event, or this or that belief of ours, and put forth statements about its authenticity. If any information comes our way to the effect that some documents may be inauthentic, we will, of course, raise that issue with the Chamber. This is our position. If Mr. McCloskey believes that the document needs to be admitted then we won't object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Gajic clarified the position on the first two documents, that he does believe they're authentic, not that there's just no evidence that they are not authentic. He's still -- and he's now told us that he doesn't object to us offering in the 12 July document that's on the screen now, but he still has not provided us his view on whether the 12 July document is authentic. Now, of course, he doesn't need to take a position on that. But I think it would be very helpful if he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this situation is quite clear now. First, the document, D183, it was MFI'd pending translation. We heard from Mr. McCloskey that there is a translation now, so that this will be in evidence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To have it clear on the record, the Registrar will make a proposal how to deal with this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Considering that the Prosecution already has uploaded original and the translation of both exhibits, D183 and D184, those exhibit numbers shall be assigned to OTP 65 ter numbers 7255 for D183; and 7256 for D184. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have all different numbers together for a single document, including the translation. There are now two documents remaining. One offered by the Prosecution; one offered by the Defence. I take it, Mr. Gajic, in page 12, line 2, you said, "We won't object to that." If there's no objection by either party, the Chamber is inclined to accept both documents. I don't see any objection by either party. Both documents will be received as exhibits. One question, Mr. McCloskey, has P2069 also a translation? It's on the screen. That's fine. Both are no longer marked for identification. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. That was actually a simple way of dealing with a complex issue. We will be providing you more information on this collection. I think it is important. There are more documents in this collection. You've -- they don't have 65 ter numbers on them. There's one reason I was reluctant to bring them and didn't do it until after they had broughten two -- brought in two. So we will have a motion for the rest to get 65 ter numbers, and in that you will see the fascinating history of these documents and where they came from and some of the difficulties associated with them. But I think that's -- that's good for now, and I should be able to finish up the re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness should be brought in. We go into closed session to enable the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning again, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. And Mr. McCloskey is continuing his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we put from yesterday page 11329 on the -- on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Witness, you'll recall from yesterday when General Tolimir was asking you about your interview with the OTP, it was -- Bruce Bursik was the investigator. And he was -- you were talking about whether -- when you had been told you were the -- a suspect. And let me look at the part that I want to ask you about. Okay. It's up there near the top and I'll read it. The question starts as: "Thank you. So until the end of your interview, you were told that you had the status of a suspect, and that's what remained?" And your answer was: "It was -- I was told so only at the end. I wasn't told at the beginning of the interview, when I asked." Now can we go to D182, that interview. And let's start with the first page, if we could. And we'll need it in this -- we'll have both languages.

utterances.speaker: PW-075 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It will take a minute or two for both languages to come up, so we can take a look in the interview and see what you think. Okay. There's page 1 of the interview. Let's go to the next page in both languages. And I'm going to read this a bit slowly. It's the bottom of the page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the bottom. Mr. Bursik the second page of the interview: "I also don't want you to ask the interpreter any questions and if you would kindly direct any questions that you have to me, the interpreter will then interpret to me the answered question." Now this is the part I want to ask you about: "Based on the information that the Tribunal has, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal believes that you may be a suspect responsible for committing acts which may be chargeable under the Tribunal Statute. Before I ask any further questions, I'm required to advise you of certain rights that you have, because you are considered to be a possible suspect. Do you understand this?" And if we flip the second page of the B/C/S you'll -- that's where it finishes up. It's page 3, the next page, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this should not be broadcast. I didn't mention it at the beginning. But the Registrar confirms that it was not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So having looked at this, when General Tolimir said to you: "So until the end of your interview you were told that you had the status of a suspect, and that's what remained," he was wrong; isn't that right? You were told right at the beginning of your interview that you were a suspect. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-075 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. Are you asking me something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, were you told you were a suspect at the beginning of the interview with Mr. Bursik?

utterances.speaker: PW-075 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I was told that. But if it says so here, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on page 11337, you made this statement yesterday. And I think I can read it without having to go to it. General Tolimir asked you if you could be held responsible basically for transporting the Muslims. And your answer was: "Well, to tell you the truth, at the time, I was even proud, in a way, that those people were able to move in an orderly fashion, safely, without being mistreated and that they were allowed to cross to the territory where they wanted to be. To me, it was logical that they were going there, and it was probably because of that, that I felt a kind of pride." You'll also recall testifying, and it was in my summary, that as soon as you got to that school you stayed a few minutes and left against the instructions of -- of Colonel Popovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-075 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Nikolic ordered me to go back immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, you did not have so much pride in what you and Popovic were doing at that school that you were willing to follow the orders of a colonel from the Drina Corps. You, instead, went back to Bratunac on the orders of a captain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to greet everybody here, the witness. May the peace reign in this house and may this trial end in accordance with God's will. The witness said that he obeyed one of the persons that he considered his superior and went back. So it's his immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour, this is an argument. I'm sorry, this is an argument.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't say that he didn't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey, please don't interrupt. You may please take off your earphones again. Mr. Tolimir, you are not in a position to testify. You may respond or object to a question of Mr. McCloskey. Please, you have the floor. Do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I objected to one part of the current conversation between the Prosecutor and the witness. He asked him why didn't you stay there, and offered a conclusion. But the witness said that he didn't stay there because Nikolic ordered him to go back and that's the only thing that I said. I simply want the things that the witness is putting us to be considered as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that is correct. We have it on the record. Page 17, line 5. "I said that Nikolic ordered me to go back immediately." That is on the record and it is the right of Mr. McCloskey now to put additional questions to that statement. Mr. McCloskey, please carry on. And witness should take the earphones on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I made the point I wanted to make. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, I want to apologise that we started very late this morning because we had to discuss many procedural matters. Now you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination here in this trial. You are free now to return to your normal activities and to go home, and the court usher will assist you. Thank you very much that you were able to come to The Hague again and to help the Chamber with your knowledge. Thank you. We turn back into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, and I -- I am very reluctant to do what I just did, but when I watched what -- to me was repeated signalling of the witness with these argumentative statements that have nothing to do with an objection. That's why I did that, objecting at that time as opposed to what we normally do and be courteous to let someone finish. And I just -- I don't know how else to handle that kind of thing when you have an important there and he's signalling him like that. But in any event, I will try to refrain that that, of course, but when it happens in important issues, I -- and I know you don't like it, and I -- I apologise to that effect. But I just don't know what else, how else to handle it. In any event, I just wanted to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If both parties would bear that in mind, that during chief examination, cross-examination and re-examination, the opposing party should be very careful to influence a witness. Not only the opposing party but also the questioning party, because we, the Chamber, have to get a full picture and we want to listen carefully to witnesses to find out what we can rely on and -- at the end of this trial. Thank you very much. Is the next witness ready to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, he is, Mr. President. Mr. Elderkin is here. And if I could be excused to say good-bye to the last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, you are excused. Welcome, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and everyone else in the courtroom. I understand that this is for the continuation of Mr. Blaszczyk's cross-examination. Before he comes in, Your Honours, I was reviewing the transcript from the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Before the witness comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it's fine if he is present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I was reviewing the witness from the end of last week with Witness David Wood and I noticed at transcript page 11106, line 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I invite the witness to sit down. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: At the reference that I just gave that I misspoke in referring to the date of a video clip, and I said a particular clip was from the 26th of July, and on review, I realize that it's from the 19th [Realtime transcript read in error "9th"] of July. I wanted to put that on the record so that that is clear. In addition, this is one of the videos which Mr. Janc will testify. Then it will be part of his testimony and hopefully we'll clear up any confusion over that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is appreciated. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I follow the proceedings in Serbian through my headphones and I also follow the transcript in English and now here at page 20, line 20, I see the mention of the 9th of July. Is it the 9th or the 19th, because I thought I heard the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Gajic is right. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And indeed I thought I said the 19th. So I certainly agree with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have the correction of the correction on the record. And it's always appreciated if you, like me, should too check the record if there are any mistakes which can create, at a later stage, some difficulties in finding out the reality. Good morning, Mr. Blaszczyk. Welcome back to the courtroom. May I remind you that the affirmation that you gave months ago in this courtroom to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing the cross-examination. Or commencing his cross-examination, if I recall correctly. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to greet everybody once again, as well as Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last time we didn't have the chance to finish the cross-examination so we are going to finish it now. My first question is: Did you investigate or did you know before you got the notebooks where they were and on whose orders were they transferred from the MUP of Serbia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I testified before, we received this information from the authorities of Republic of Serbia, and they inform us also where the notebooks were found. If this is your question. But before that, we didn't know about the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that you didn't know. I wanted to ask you whether you investigated where those notebooks were before they were seized by the MUP of Serbia and before they came into your possession. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We have no information when -- where the notebooks were before they were seized by the Serbian MUP and before we got it from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaszczyk. Did you personally, as an OTP investigator, while reviewing the notebooks, find out whether something was erased from the notebooks or whether some additional notes were made subsequently in the notebooks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my reviewing of the notebooks, I didn't notice anything unusual that something was erased from the notebook or was added later on. For me, the notebooks looks authentical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you investigate where those notebooks were during the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that the notebooks in the war were in the possession of General Mladic, and ... I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you whether you investigated it. Then you can say that you did or that you did not investigate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was obvious for us that they were in the possession of General Mladic. And we see from the video, for example, from Potocari, or from Bratunac, or from Zepa, from Boksanica. Especially this notebook related to 1995, July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you investigate why those notebooks were not given to you earlier and whether they were present earlier in the buildings which were searched, as well as whether there were any searches made before the search which yielded the notebooks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I tried to explain the situation. Also I was wondering why these notebooks were not seized during the first search made by the Serbian MUP before the proper search, let's say. And their explanation was that they didn't find these notebooks at that time because they were not concentrated or -- and they seized any documents from -- from this house from this apartment. They were more concentrated to find whether there is General Mladic at that time, to check whether he is over there. And regarding the 17 notebooks seized in 2010, according to information we received from MUP, these notebooks, these 17 notebooks, were hidden in -- in house, were not seized during the first search, the proper search for the documents, which was done in 2008, December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just said it was in December. But, tell us, did you investigate how many searches of the house of General Mladic were conducted before the notebooks were found? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, how many searches was done -- were done in the house of General Mladic, but at least two or three times before, the MUP was in this house. Before December 2008. But I don't remember right now off the top of my head, no, how many times they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, sir, can you tell us now where the original notebooks are and whether they will be returned to their owner, once the OTP has copied them and used in accordance with the procedure applied to things found in searches? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is question not to me. I cannot say whether these notebooks can be returned to the owner of these -- of these notebooks when the proceeding is over here in the Tribunal. But, so far, we have all the originals here in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what the procedures are that are applied by the Tribunal regarding the return of objects seized on the occasion of searches? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These particular notebooks, they are evidence, Tribunal evidence, evidence you are keeping these -- these -- these notebooks here in our evidence unit in The Hague. And what would be the fate of the archive later on of the evidence unit, really, I am not fully aware what is going to happen to this archive, to the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The archives of Serbia or the Republika Srpska or the VRS, or, rather, items taken from there, will they ever be returned; and what is the position of the OTP in that regard? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer would be the same. I am not aware what is going to happen to this evidence after the Tribunal is closed. But, so far, these documents are treated as evidence here in the Tribunal, and these documents have to be kept in our evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if the originals in the possession of the OTP, seized by the OTP were -- or, rather, whether certificates were issued to the owners about the seizure of the originals? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If OTP seize any documents wherever, you know, definitely the investigators, whoever seized the documents, they are issued a certificate, yes, to the owner of the documents. We did, for example, in case of documents from Fontana Hotel, of documents seized in the Fontana Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was, in this case, a certificate issued for temporarily dispossessed items, or was it a certificate of permanent seizure? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, together with my investigator, my colleague investigator, we -- we issued a certificate of permanent seizure, or confirmation, whatever, you know, whatever we seized over there, we issued a certificate to the person who was responsible for the documents from Fontana Hotel, who were guarding the documents. It's too big of a word, for example, to use just he was in possession of the documents. He was guarding the Fontana hotel, and we issued a certificate to him that we seized these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please remind the Trial Chamber about the nature of the documents found at the Fontana Hotel and whether they are documents that constitute part of these notebooks about which you're testifying today?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These documents are not the part of the notebooks. I used the Fontana Hotel as example, just what we did when we seize, the OTP seized some documents. I refer to Fontana Hotel because I personally participated in seizure of the documents from Fontana Hotel. But these documents from Fontana Hotel are not the part of the notebook at all. Just they are receipts, they are as far as I remember, they are information, you know, how many people stayed in Fontana Hotel, who used rooms in Fontana Hotel in interested period for us at that time. But they are not connected to the Mladic notebooks at all. I used this information as a sample what we did with the documents seized by us. But if, in regards to the documents seized by -- by local authority, like in Serbia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, wherever, we are not issuing them any -- any certificate or whatever, you know, to the owner of these documents. It was done exclusively by the people, by the authorities who seized these documents. In the case of -- of -- of Mladic notebook, it was Serbian MUP who issued certificate to the owner of -- in fact, not to the owner, but to the family of Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us forget the Fontana case, because it is unrelated. Let's not confuse the Tribunal. Tell us, what difference do you see between documents seized by the MUP, and those seized by the Tribunal? Since they are in the possession of the Tribunal, do they have any sort of document that they issued to the owner?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the notebooks, the notebooks were seized by the Serbian MUP, by Serbian authority in Belgrade. They issued a certification to the person who kept this material at his accommodation and where -- where the material was seized. In this case, it was Bosiljka Mladic, wife of General Mladic, and also his son, Darko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are interested in the legal status of these documents. That's why let us see P1389. It is in e-court and let us see whether these documents are seized or confiscated. Thank you. Now we see on the first page of both linguistic versions, it's a document of the Ministry of Interior of Serbia. It is a -- it's titled: "Confirmation regarding temporarily seized items." And that's what it says in Serbian too. Here's my question. Since this is a certificate of temporarily seized items, rather than confiscated items, tell me, is there a legal deadline for returning temporarily seized items to their rightful owner? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have been informed by the Prosecution that they have rules that they should after, I believe, after 90 days they should return all the seized material to the owner of this material. But it was made clear to the Office of the Prosecutor from Serbia that this material will be in the possession of the Tribunal till at least till the end of the ending of the proceeding here in the Tribunal. And, in fact, recently I have been remind by the Prosecution office from Serbia to send additional information, how long or whether we are going still to keep these documents in -- here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, is there a ruling of the Tribunal to the effect that -- a ruling in this particular case, to the effect that the items are permanently confiscated, which means that they will not be returned within 90 days? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you are referring to this notebook? General Ratko Mladic notebooks?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That is precisely what we're talking about. It says here, "temporarily seized". Which means that they should be returned within 90 days. What is the procedure applied if the 90-days' deadline is not observed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure is in such a way that, as I said, just a few seconds ago that I have been remind by the Serbian authorities that I should send additional information that those notebooks is not going to be returned right now to Serbia. We are going to keep these notebooks here at least until the end of the proceedings by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us now why this is so, given the fact that all electronic documents have been made based on the notebooks and nothing can be changed anymore?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference between the originals and between the scanned version of the documents. Always the best evidence are the original evidence, not the scanned version or second copy of whatever. You know, just document. The best evidence are originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, then, if the one in whose possession the original is can alter the original and then claim that the original is the most trustworthy source? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are talking about the notebooks, it's not possible, and I don't believe that any alteration can be done with these notebooks while they are here in the Tribunal in our evidence unit, preserved by trained people who are working in the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it a rule that one of the parties to the proceedings has the monopoly over the documents and the evidence used in the trial? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean saying "monopoly". The evidence kept at the evidence unit are for the disposal of OTP as well as Defence. If Defence wants to look, for example at some documents, these documents are accessible, the originals are accessible for them. And for them and also for Trial Chamber. The OTP has not exclusive custody of these documents. It is not OTP. The evidence unit is a part -- is independent part, you know, not a part of OTP, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give us information if this material is accessible to both the Prosecution and the Defence on an equal basis? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see big difference. Definitely we -- easier for us to get access to this material because evidence unit is located in this building, even in my floor, at least one of the vaults. And if I need to get originals, I am just submitting request to evidence unit. They are signing out documents to me, and I'm getting access to these documents. With Defence, probably I don't know exactly the procedure, but several time I received also request from Defence that they would like to see the originals, and probably easier through us, you know, just inform the investigators that Defence would like to see the particular documents, original document, and we are submitting this request to evidence unit. Evidence unit is signing out the documents to us, and we are showing these documents to the Defence people or whoever would like to see these documents from other parties. But, definitely, Defence has no limited access to these documents. If they want to see these documents, the originals, there's no problem at all. I don't see any problem why not. And I never met situation that they never -- they -- their request has been denied or not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for what you said. Please tell us, does the service that has custody over this material part of the OTP, which would make you -- which would make it easier for you to access that material than for the Defence, which has to go through you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, Your Honour, I am not sure whether evidence unit is the part of OTP. Could be the part of registry. But I can be wrong. For example, the witness section is part of registry. But, yes, yes, we are working closer to the evidence unit because we are the person, I mean, the OTP let's say, this is the body who are submitting evidence to -- to the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaszczyk. It wasn't my intention to ask you questions that you -- or, rather, to which you cannot provide full answers. The Trial Chamber can establish that and see to it that equal conditions prevail. You or I cannot do anything about that. Here's my following question: Have you ever considered in the OTP when the material will be returned to its rightful owner; and has any decision been reached about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware about any decision about that, but, for sure, management has to decide what we can do after the Tribunal is closed, after the proceeding is -- is over, what to do with the archive and with -- especially with the evidence and with the original material kept in our evidence unit. I believe this is still in process, you know, just what to do with this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But somebody else has authority there. It's in somebody else's remit. But tell me, do you distinguish between diary and notebook; and, if so, what do you mean by either term? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it can be distinction between diary and notebooks. Notebooks are used, you know, just to make notes, just during the meetings. The diary is -- is also the notebook, but conducted -- or just where the person is putting -- putting information on daily basis. And telling information on daily basis from his activity, not only from his meetings but whatever he is doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are we talking about documents that were created and that reflect the thoughts of the one who created them, the thoughts and feelings, or do they contain facts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be both, you know, it could be thoughts, and also containing the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why don't you use the same term then? If they are notebooks, then you will agree with me that they should be called notebooks and not diaries, because a diary can be of a very subjective nature. Something in which the author of the diary enters his or her thoughts and feelings, right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, this is a matter of using the word, you know, "diary" or "notebooks". But it is visible if you look at the notebooks, these particular notebooks of General Mladic, he is putting the facts over there, he is putting the meetings. He is saying who participated in the meetings and who said what said. This type of information over there. Whether we use the term diary -- maybe we are wrong, but it is, rather, notebooks. Maybe you are right. Mostly they are facts in these documents, these Ratko Mladic notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an investigator, please tell us whether you distinguished between what was entered in the notebook as fact and what was entered as opinion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had the time to analyse all collection of these notebooks. I mostly concentrated on the notebooks from 1995, but in this notebook most of the material they are facts, you know, put by General Mladic. They are information about meetings, about the people who participated during the meetings and what was said during these particular meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us the following: You can enter in a notebook what happened, but in a diary you can also describe what happened. What is the difference? And did you, as an investigator, go into that regarding some entries in the documents which have been temporarily seized? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would say that the notebooks seized from family of General Mladic, I never made such investigation, just whatever, you know, just tried to distinguish these notebooks or just to make investigation whether these notebooks are more diaries or notebooks itself. But, for me, they are containing more facts than -- than thoughts of -- of General Mladic. In this context, it would be rather, notebooks - you're right - not diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this trial there are court reporters. They record every word spoken by the Judges, you, me, and so on. And journalists report and add their subjective opinions and conclusions, and that's how they inform the public. What is more trustworthy? The record made by the court reporter or a journalist report which reflects the essence what happened but does not offer a complete record? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having exact record, what has been said, is better because you can easily came to your own conclusion what was said, or to what -- what is going on exactly, you know, just what the meeting was about, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's time for our first break. We have to adjourn, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Blaszczyk, we left it off just as I was about to ask you whether you investigated or analysed the possibility of personal entries made in the notebooks. My question is this: If a person is merely documenting the positions stated by another, is there the possibility of presenting one's own view, in that case, minimal?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there is possibility. Depends, you know, what the person understood from -- from -- from the words from another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless somebody is a stenographer and wishes to take down everything said in this courtroom, for example, do -- does such a person have any room for subjective thoughts instead of being able to transcribe accurately what each and every person stated?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are referring to General Mladic notebooks, the entry from these notebooks, it is possible, of course, that General Mladic was not professional stenographer, but whatever he put in these notebooks is visible that it -- he put what he understood from -- from -- from another person who -- who were present during this meeting, for example. But how he understood it, of course, this is other -- other -- other thing. Whether he correctly recorded what -- with a -- what his person with whom he had conversation passed to him or not, this is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If someone is writing a diary, as opposed to making entries in a notebook, is the possibility of presenting one's own views, conclusions, and interpretations even greater?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone is writing a diary, he can put in diary whatever he wants. He can put whatever, his thoughts, his -- information about his private life. Whatever he wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this, please: When taking over the notebooks, did the OTP receive any restrictions from the MUP of Serbia regarding any confidential use of the whole or parts of the material, precisely for the reasons we have just been discussing?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in touch with the Serbian MUP, with the Serbian authorities, and we got -- they were informed that we were going to use these notebooks and entire contents of the notebooks in the court proceedings here in the Tribunal. There was no condition from the Serbian MUP, you know, how to use these notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any conditions put that some parts be used in private instead of open session? You realize that we move into private or closed session here, if there are protective measures applied to a witness. Were any such requests of that nature put forth by the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of such request. I don't remember, at least. I don't -- I don't think that I -- I saw such requests from the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that any request a state had to do -- had to make of the Tribunal would be known to you? To the -- to the OTP, that is to say.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's -- if there was such request, for sure it would be -- would be known to the OTP, to the Tribunal. It should be sent to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you review the entire correspondence between the Serbian MUP and the Committee for Cooperation with the Tribunal and this Tribunal, so as to furnish the complete information covered by my question?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I reviewed all the material, all the correspondence between the Serbian MUP and -- and the Tribunal related to these particular searches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean that the State of Serbia and its bodies did not seek any data protection used before the Tribunal, regardless of whether such data is about individuals or institutions?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we are talking about the entry from Ratko Mladic notebooks, or generally about documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking about the documents that are introduced through you, such as the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember at the beginning, there was discussion about -- about confidentiality of this material at the time when the material was seized and handed over to the Tribunal. But later on, it was made clear to the -- to the Serbian side that this material is going to be used in the court in -- in the court proceeding here but I am not aware about any -- any restriction made by the Serbian -- by the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did the Serbian state put any conditions before us as the participants of these proceedings to use the material introduced through you? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware about any conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether in other cases the hearing is moved into closed session when reference is made to some material provided by Serbia which is considered state secrets, such as meetings of the Supreme Defence Council, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we go into private session for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise to the Registrar, and I'd like to thank Mr. Elderkin for his remark. I merely used that as a general example without stipulating any specific data about the persons appearing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us this, please, since you were interrupted in your answer. I asked you whether you knew that in some other proceedings before this Tribunal data provided by Serbia is protected; for example, when it comes to the meetings of the Serbian state leadership, attended, among others, by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow another proceedings, to be honest. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you in a position to receive answers to all the questions we refer to so that we could have a clear position during these proceedings and the use of material, given the fact that we, as citizens of Serbia, have to abide by the requests and instructions provided by the Serbian government?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends of kind of question you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
