utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a brief summary of Dr. Tabeau's prior testimony that I would like to read into the record. Dr. Tabeau testified in the case of The Prosecutor v. Vujadin Popovic et al. on 5 February 2008. Dr. Tabeau holds a Ph.D. in mathematical demography from the Warsaw School of Economics and is a demographer by profession. She was employed by the ICTY, beginning in 2000, and has worked as the project leader of the Demographic Unit since. Dr. Tabeau's work encompasses the study of the demographic consequences of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, and, in particular, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. She has prepared numerous expert reports for court and maintains an information system on the victims of the conflict, killed persons, missing persons, and displaced persons. In January 2008, Dr. Tabeau produced a report entitled: "The Srebrenica Missing: 2007 Progress Report on the DNA-Based Identification by ICMP." Based on records provided by the ICMP showing DNA matches for Srebrenica-related victims, the report updated a 16 November 2005 report and list concerning the missing and dead from Srebrenica. The 2007 progress report effectively summarized the statistics for identified persons and cross-referenced the list of identified individuals provided by the ICMP against the November 2005 OTP list. In addition, the report examined the list of unique DNA profiles provided by the ICMP. During her testimony, Dr. Tabeau discussed the methodology used to prepare the report, which is set out in the November 2005 report and has been consistently applied by the Demographics Unit. In particular, Dr. Tabeau explained the methodology used to assess the quality of the information upon which the report was based and the process of matching the cross-referenced lists that were used. This process involved, inter alia, checking the names, first, family, and father's names, dates of birth and controlling for duplicate records. Several other criteria were also used. Similar criteria was used to check for duplicate records in the ICMP data in which some information deficiencies were initially observed, typically as between reassociations and main cases and in relation to protocol numbers. These discrepancies were subsequently clarified by the ICMP, resulting in good and reliable data for analytical purposes. Based on the analysis of the ICMP data at the time, the number of main cases through 4 October 2007 was 4263, representing discreet DNA profiles. There were 2346 reassociated cases, that is, secondary DNA match to a main case. And 3837 individuals on the November 2005 OTP list were matched to the ICMP list of DNA-identified individuals. This represented around 90 per cent of the ICMP records and approximately 50 per cent of the November 2005 OTP list. Some 10 per cent of the ICMP list entries were found to be "less certain matches," either because only names could be matched without more, such as complete dates of birth on either ICMP records or ICRC records, or because more than one name was alternatively attributed to a given DNA profile, as was the case with missing siblings. Finally, there were some records that could not be matched to any extent. Dr. Tabeau noted, however, that while there is never a one-to-one relationship among various missing persons lists, there tends to be a large overlap or common part. In comparing Dean Manning's 2007 report to the 2007 progress report in terms of the total number of Srebrenica-related victims found in grave-sites, Dr. Tabeau attributed differences in the findings to narrower criteria used by Manning in the selection of grave-sites for analysis. She noted that Manning did not include grave-sites containing mixed remains, but only those containing remains exclusively related to Srebrenica. These sites are recognised by the ICTY and accepted as such. However, the OTP list did include the remains of mixed graves and relied on ICMP data in respect of defining additional Srebrenica-related graves. In order to eliminate the possibility of counting survivors among the missing and dead, the November 2005 report compared data against several lists, including the population census, the voters' registers for 1997, 1998 and 2000, as well as the official register of internally displaced persons and refugees from 2000. This was ultimately retained in the 2007 progress report. Similarly, as BiH army records were not used in producing the 2005 November report, they were not relied on in the 2007 progress report, which listed a total of 7.661 Srebrenica-related missing and dead. That concludes my summary, Mr. President, and I have some questions for Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this quite lengthy summary. You may go ahead with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Can I have, please, 65 ter 7172 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, you heard me mention a little bit about your educational background in mathematical demography. Can you tell us, just briefly, what that is and whether or not you apply that in relation to the work that you're doing now.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Mathematical demography is a subarea of demography. Demography belongs to social sciences. I studied statistics and econometrics as my major subjects and graduated with the masters degree in economics. In my Ph.D., I completed a project that was based on the use of mathematical models in the analysis of demographic issues, and my degree in -- based on this dissertation was seen as Ph.D. in mathematical demography. It is a quantitative subfield of demographic analysis of the population, simply studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I noticed well, first of all, can you tell us what we have in e-court so we're clear for the record?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is my CV, the brief version of my CV. First page, basic information about me and my education and degrees and my work experience. It also summarizes my competencies. I consider myself specialist in statistics, inferential and descriptive. I'm specialist in handling deficient data sources, such as surveys, population surveys, population census, other sources. I'm also an expert in modelling techniques and other areas of demography and statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I noticed in your CV that you sent some time working for the Netherlands Interdisciplinary Demographic Institute?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I worked there approximately nine years, between the year 1991 and the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what kind of work were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This institute is the national demographic institute of the Netherlands. I was -- there, I was conducting scientific research of mortality, mortality in developed countries, in Western countries of Europe and Central European countries. My research area included forecasting of mortality and studying prospects for life expectancy. Also the study of mortality by cause of death, longevity. So that was basically the nine years before coming to the Tribunal, I was doing this kind of research.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And one other thing I'd like to ask you about is your work for the Extraordinary Chambers of the Courts of Cambodia. Here it is indicated between May and September of 2009. Can you tell us a little bit about what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. It was a project I completed as you mentioned in the second half of 2009, at the invitation of investigative judges of the Khmer Rouge Tribunal. In this project, I provided an assessment of the victims of the Khmer Rouge regime in Cambodia. This report is meant to be used in court proceedings in the upcoming casings in the Tribunal in Phnom Penh. It is an expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does your CV contain a list of publications that you have done?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The second page contains a selection of publications and research reports and expert reports that I have written. The complete CV contains many more, but the selection here are the most recent papers. So if we could see the second page on the -- and the third page, perhaps, then we will see that there are a number of titles I, so far in the past ten years, I was able to produce approximately 40 expert reports for the ICTY cases. Of course, there is the expert report for Khmer Rouge Tribunal. There are -- there is a special issue of the Journal of the European Demographers. There is a book on demography of war, published by Springer. There are several articles published in international journals. So I am saying it is just a selection of the latest papers. There is a third page, I think, that we are not seeing right now in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. The court recorder is requesting that you slow down while speaking, especially you are using different terms which are quite difficult to record. Please slow down while speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am very sorry. I'm very sorry. Perhaps I should repeat what I was saying. There are several categories of publications presented in this CV. There is a number of expert reports completed most recently for ICTY cases. There will be monographs, and next category included here, on the first place, there is a book that was published by Springer about demography of war, that I edited jointly with Helge Brunborg and Henrik Urdal from Norway. There are also other monographs, including a book published recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down. You have the same speed again. It is very difficult and you are referring to different names and different languages. Please a little bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The book was -- the book by Springer was edited jointly by me with Helge Brunborg and Henrik Urdal. These are researchers from Norway and the title of the book is demography of war. There is another book. It is a book containing a selection of public expert reports from ICTY cases. This book was published by the Helsinki Committee of Serbia in Belgrade. There are two language versions; one English, one Serbo-Croat. There is a special issue of a journal of the European demographers, "The European Journal of Population". I edited this special issue, again, with some co-authors, in this case just one, Helge Brunborg. And there is an expert report among monographs, the assessment report of the Bosnian Book of Death. That is the largest existing database on victims of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina compiled by a local NGO from Sarajevo headed by Mirsad Tokaca. This assessment was made at the question of Ambassador of Norway and Switzerland and of Tokaca, himself. And the last portion of my papers, selected papers included here are some articles, journal articles, and some more are just conference papers. Because it is all on record. I don't think I will be going through it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I would like to tender this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the number again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7172 shall be assigned exhibit number P2081. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand there is not a translation for it yet but one has been requested. So in keeping with the practice of the -- of the Chamber, perhaps it should be marked for identification, pending that translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we will mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, you -- well, we can see a number of expert reports that you have produced in a number of cases. Let me ask, have you been qualified as an expert in proceedings before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. I appeared in the capacity of an expert witness 16 times in various trials, including the trial of Popovic, from 2008 but also other trials, Slobodan Milosevic, Vojislav Seselj. I also testified in Sarajevo cases, that is, General Galic, General Dragomir Milosevic. I testified recently in Stanisic and Simatovic and the other Stanisic case, that is, Stanisic-Zupljanin case. I also testified as an expert in Herceg-Bosna, Prlic et al. case, and several other cases, so the complete record is 16 expert testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now in your work at the ICTY, when you started in 2000, you became the project leader, as I understand it, for the Demographic Unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us, basically, what duties and responsibilities you had in that role?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The major responsibility was to produce demographic expert reports that -- for use in the ICTY trials. I was working as a Prosecution witness, so the Prosecution perspective was represented in these reports, but more generally, the reports were always made with the idea of fair representation of all affected victims. Further, my responsibility was to collect information sources, in particular, statistical sources, on the consequences of the wars in the former Yugoslavia. A particular type of consequences were, of course, demographic consequences of the wars. Bosnia and Herzegovina was our first priority, so collection of sources implied the next responsibility, organisation of information system that can be used in the OTP for the needs of demographic analysis and then the other needs of trials. So, generally, this unit has operated as a small statistical office in the Office of the Prosecutor, but predominantly the first and most important task was producing the expert reports, demographic expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a little bit about the background related to the April 2009 report and the missing list. You are familiar with that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, that is P1776 and P1777.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask first -- maybe we should get the first one up on the screen. That would be P1776, just so you can see what I'm talking about. All right, I think you recognise what is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is the 2009 report that I've just referred to, is it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the most current progress report concerning Srebrenica-related missing and dead as well as the list that accompanies it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as one of its authors, can you just remind us what the report is intended to show. And I mean in a very brief, if you can, and simple way, because I know it contains a lot of information. And you will remember that Dr. Brunborg has already given evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This report relates to the victims of the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995. It is meant as a background report that would be showing the scale of victimisation, first of all, in terms of the reported missing persons, related to the fall, and, secondly, also, in terms of identified persons. The term "identified persons" in this context is very important while -- whereas, for the missing persons a list can be made with all kind of details. This list is no more than just a list of missing persons. The identified persons is a different category. It is a category that relates to the human remains exhumed from the mass graves and other graves in the territory of Srebrenica and neighbouring municipalities in Eastern Bosnia. For the identified persons, the DNA matching reports are available. So this report is a integration of these two perspectives, one perspective is the missing persons, the second perspective is the identified persons, DNA-identified persons. By cross-referencing these two categories, or generally speaking, these two lists of persons, a clearer picture emerges of the overlap between the two, of how the two perspectives corroborate each other. So the whole concept of this report is to show our initial list of missing persons enlarged by integration of the latest information on the DNA matching of Srebrenica victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Let me just focus on the first part of this analysis, and that has to do with the missing persons as distinguished from the identified persons? In terms of establishing a list, an OTP list, of missing persons, can you tell us what basic data sources you relied on in order to do that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For establishing of missing persons list, we used the lists compiled by ICRC, International Committee for Red Cross, various editions. The latest edition that we used for 2009 report was the 2008, as far as I remember, edition of the ICRC reports. Secondly, the second type of lists were the -- was the list prepared by American organisation, Physician for Human Rights, but this component in the latest report became very small. It is predominantly the ICRC list of missing persons for Bosnia and Herzegovina as the major source for the list as such. It doesn't mean that no other sources were used as contextual for this list or supportive. If I can go a little longer on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one thing while we're on the topic. You mentioned -- you mentioned that you used various editions of the ICRC lists, and in particular, the most recent one was 2008. Can you tell us why various editions of the ICRC list were used?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The ICRC didn't stop their work on registration of missing persons. Soon after the war ended they have continued this work until the present time. So the latest list that we acquired from October 2008 is the best we -- we -- the most recent, the best we can have and this is why we used it. Moreover, this particular list from October 2008 was a list particularly compiled for Srebrenica victims which makes it different from other lists that were covering the entire country, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You made use of the census --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That is correct. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- in respect of establishing this list. Can you tell us what purpose that was for?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That census, as such, is not a source that was used to make the list. It was a source that we used to cross-reference our list of Srebrenica missing, to validate the records, simply speaking, to confirm that these individuals did, indeed, were -- live in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the outbreak of the conflict and to improve the information, personal information about the victims. The census is a very rich source of information and we, in this way, could learn a lot about the victims, including their ethnicity. Ethnicity is important and is, unfortunately, unavailable from the ICRC list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of your use of the voter registration, my understanding is that you used voter registrations, or voter registers I should say, for 1997, 1998 and 2000. First of all, is that right?

We used these lists in order to eliminate false positives in case if there would be records of missing persons overlapping with the records of survivors, post-war survivors, then, of course, this would give good reasons to reconsider the inclusion of certain cases of missing persons in our list of Srebrenica missing. So it was the elimination of false positives. That was the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the voter registrations list, to your knowledge was there such a list available in 1996, immediately after the cessation of the hostilities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU

There were certain problems related to the 1996 election. Cases of fraud were frequently addressed. So I -- there was no registration of voters who wanted to -- to vote. utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned the use, in your prior testimony, of a list of internally displaced persons. First, can you tell us what that is; and then how you used it.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is it yet another source on the survivors of the war. This list of internally displaced persons and refugees is simply a registration system of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and UNHCR, a system that was actually operating already during the war, but after the war, the UNHCR considerably improved the registration and the electronic system which resulted that a large database of IDPs and refugees in Bosnia and Herzegovina became available in the year 2000. The number of cases registered in this system is 508.000 of cases, almost 600.000 individuals, most of them being the internally displaced persons, and we were able to acquire these records for the use in the OTP and also in this particular report, 2009 report on Srebrenica victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in terms of your analysis of this material, in your prior testimony you mentioned some fundamentals concerning the matching criteria that you used. If you could, and I know there is a section of this in your report, if you could explain in a nutshell what that process involves. Let's start with, for example, how many matching criteria you considered in order to use this data effectively?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In order to understand the importance of matching, it is important to stress that we have been working with individual records representing persons, so record of information is a set of data items that describe a given person. In order to trace a person's fate, starting at the outbreak of the war, throughout the war, and later, after the war, it is necessary to match sources with each other using the individual data items reported for every person. Matching is also called linking of records. Another term used for matching is cross-referencing of sources. So what we basically do in our work, in the work of my unit, is every person, be it a victim or a -- I mean, killed person, missing person, detained person, or a displaced person, this person is first identified in our core source, that is the population census of 1991, and starting from there we can check using the matching how the person is reported and whether the person is reported in any other source. Matching in statistics is usually done, if possible, using numeric characteristics, that would be record numbers for instance, or personal identification numbers. If they are reported in the compared or cross-referenced sources then matching is limited to searching for the same personal ID as reported in the census in any other source. That is the simplest variant the matching, which however is not always possible. In many sources, especially on sources related to victims, such personal identification numbers are unavailable. So matching must be based on different criteria. Predominantly on descriptive criteria, descriptive, including, for example, names of persons, surname, first name, father's name; date of birth; place of birth; place of residence; et cetera, et cetera. So matching becomes a complex process as the descriptive characteristics are sometimes difficult to compare. If you think of problems that can be associated with reporting of persons in various sources, like, for instance, spelling of names, completeness of dates, reporting of place names, these are all challenges that must be overcome, in order to proceed successfully with matching. Matching based on descriptive characteristics is not uncommon in today's world. In statistical offices like US Bureau of Census this kind of matching is quite common. Why? Because the personal identification number is often not reported in various sources. So matching has to be done based on names and other personal details. There exists various forms of matching, machine-based matching, for instance, exists that would involve artificial intelligence and there are other forms of matching. The other spectrum would include rule-based approaches. Rule based means that decisions about declaring the true match are made by a human expert. And this is the kind of approach that we have taken at this Tribunal. So we don't rely on automated matching in 100 per cent of our cases. Whenever possible, we do the automated matching. In other cases, when automated matching is impossible, or too risky, we use the rule-based approach, with human expert deciding on the possibility to declare a match -- a true or non-true match.

If could you tell us a little bit about, in as brief terms as possible, why those databases were not used, that would be helpful?

Thank you. We have in our hands two large databases, one obtained from the statistical authority of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and another one obtained from the statistical authority of the RS, Republika Srpska. Both databases are large. The two together comprise 140.000 individual records, each representing a death, a case of death, during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1992 to 1995. These databases were compiled based on -- on the death notifications made by the families of the deceased to the statistical authority. This is the death records that also in normal time, in peace, are usually collected and processed by statistical authority. In order to make an entry it is necessary for the statistical authority to have a document, in most cases a death certificate, based on which the person is registered in the death register. In our project on Srebrenica, we -- it wasn't our purpose to compile a complete list of persons who died in the fall of Srebrenica in 1995. Our focus has always been the missing persons, the missing persons and, subsequently, the plan was to link the missing with exhumation records. This approach is because of a belief the OTP, and, I think, of our own, that missing persons, unfortunately and sadly, are, in most cases, confirmed in the exhumation records. So this is a very special group of victims which actually we concentrated on in our work. Obviously these kind of records, records of missing persons, cannot be entered and accepted by statistical authority to register as in the statistical system. As for the missing persons, the important document confirming the death, the death certificate, is unavailable, obviously. The body is unavailable, and there is no rationale for registering these cases. So this is my explanation related to the two major sources, large sources available at the OTP that were not used in our work. There was one more source that we didn't use, a source that is large that I mentioned already today, this source. This is the so-called Bosnian Book of Death. It is the largest existing list or database on victims of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the entire country, beginning in April 1992, until the end of 1995. This database shortly, BBD, as we call it, BBD, is a -- comprises at this stage approximately 100.000 cases, which is believed to be almost complete in terms of victims of war. The databases -- this database was compiled in Sarajevo by a local NGO called Research and Documentation Centre. It is a human rights NGO headed by Mirsad Tokaca, and database is a result of the work of this NGO, years-long work, with regard to collecting information on deaths and missing persons and maintaining -- establishing and maintaining a database. Well, this is not a database that should be seen as a statistical standard. It is a product of a NGO and there are a number of issues related to this work, although, generally, this database is seen as a very important and positive product. But, as a matter of fact, one of the deficiencies of the database is that records have been edited constantly by -- when entering -- when making new entries. The editing of records leads to integrating various sources in one record and makes it impossible to track original source for every data item. What I'm trying to say, the database become -- has become a source in itself, and it is not that it is a very straightforward thing to link it back to the actual sources used. In our work, this is a very serious problem because whatever list is presented in a court of law we must be able to justify our sources, to assess the sources, to eliminate any bias, possible bias included, simply we must have a 100 percent transparency in presenting our list of victims, and that is not really possible when working with the BBD.

Yes, it is the same -- the same list and the same table that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just before we go forward, Mr. President, I'd like to tender that document, that's 65 ter 7252. If you would like, I can put it on the screen so we can all have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, no, we have seen it already. But I take it that you are moving for leave to add this to document to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is a fair question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I don't see an objection by the Defence. Am I correct? Again, I saw in the list at the end, this remark "with leave of the Trial Chamber." Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We didn't receive --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, I didn't receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was your own translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted and the document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7252 shall be assigned exhibit number P2082. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question to the witness at this point in time. We have seen this list which we have on the screen now already earlier. Can you give us your opinion how it came that in the DOD military column that there are some dates from 1992, 1993, and 1994, which were later corrected? What might be the reason, taking into your account your experience with these data, for stating by the military of BiH, the date of disappearance or date of death prior to 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is good to note that these kind of systems are dynamic, so the version that we have of these military records was made at some point, and it is not necessarily so that all the records included in this list have been updated. It is possible that during the war certain individuals were reported as disappeared in 1992, 1993, 1994, long before Srebrenica happened, the fall of Srebrenica. And nobody has ever corrected this information. This happens. This happens frequently. We are speaking of a wartime registration, a war situation is a special situation. Many structures that work in peace normally don't work normally during war. So these kind of omissions, I would call it even not an error, an omission and lack of updating of information, leads eventually to seeing these kind of inconsistencies. So this is not the only source in which these kind of problems I noticed, so that would be the most straightforward explanation of the issue. So using the actual current-day status, the authorities have possibilities to check what is the current-day status of certain persons reported earlier as missing, and it is perfectly possible that they could have provide -- have provided us with corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I appreciate that. I do have here 65 ter 2770 that I'd like to show the witness. I understand there's not a translation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But can you just tell us for the record, so that is clear to General Tolimir, what this is.

This is a RFA, our Request for Assistance, that was sent in June 2004 to the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this RFA, we request, for 142 persons, to provide us with information about their place of death, cause of death, and further confirmation of the date of death. I already mentioned this RFA earlier today in the context of the memorandum that we are discussing. And here it is, we have it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 2770 shall be assigned exhibit number P2083, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 2771.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Tabeau, in respect of the RFA that you just testified about, was there any request, to your knowledge, made by the OTP for the Ministry of Defence or the Bosnian authorities to change or correct any of the dates of death or disappearance or place of death or disappearance with respect to any one of the 142 persons indicated in that RFA?
In response to this RFA, we obtained corrections for 127 individuals out of initially requested number of 142 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt for a moment. Is there an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The translation is actually on the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we should have it on the screen as well. Thank you. Sorry for interrupting. Please continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question was, Dr. Tabeau, whether or not any request was made by the OTP, to your knowledge, or anybody else, to have the Bosnian authorities, the Bosnian Ministry of Defence, change or correct the place of death, cause of death, or -- or dates relating to either, concerning the 142 individuals referenced in the RFA.

It wasn't our request that they would correct an information in their systems. It was our request to obtain information about certain characteristics of the cases that we sent them, the characteristics, including the date of death, place of death. So that was our request, it wasn't -- why would we correct their databases? Of course, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you receive that information in response to the RFA?

Yes, we received a number of records, documents mentioning the correct date of disappearance or death, and place of disappearance or death for quite a number of cases so that we could use this information in our revising, or not, the cases that we already had on our list of Srebrenica missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that the subject of this response? In other words, did you get that information as a result of -- or as contained in this response?

Yes, of course. Yes, that is the subject, and in the 127 cases, the information obtained from the federal Ministry of Defence corroborated the information that we had from the ICRC regarding these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to tender this document as well, Mr. President. 65 ter 2771.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall be assigned exhibit number P2084. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Lastly, Dr. Tabeau, I had some questions concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to put forth a remark. The Defence used this same document during the cross-examination of the witness Brunborg. This is 65 ter 1D137. So I think that the record should contain the information that this document was used previously; although, of course, now it bears a different number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Always helpful to all numbers together to be able to link them. But if I recall correctly, we postponed a decision about that. It was marked for identification or not; I don't recall. Perhaps you can help us with that. If you used it with Mr. Brunborg, I think it should have been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the time, we did not request that this document be tendered into evidence because we also intended to use it with this witness. Our use with Mr. Brunborg was rather limited. Maybe you would recall that we were talking about certain documents relating to certain persons, and information such as age and the exact date of disappearance between Srebrenica and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now it is clear. We have P2084 on the screen. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Lastly, Dr. Tabeau, I wanted to ask you about certain information that was provided to you from a book that was published by Milivoje Ivanisevic. And concerned some 58 names of individuals that was broached by the Defence during the testimony of Dr. Brunborg. First, do you know what I'm talking about?
Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Second, have you had an opportunity to look at these names or review these names against the OTP missing list?

Yes, I did. I -- these are my preliminary observations that I will be talking about. The work is not yet finished. But I did cross-reference this list with the OTP of -- the OTP list of Srebrenica missing of 2009, and the conclusion is these records do, indeed, match the records of the missing persons. There are a few inconsistencies. I cannot say that every record can be matched with 100 percent consistency. I also tried to match the 58 names with other sources, with the census, for instance, of 1991. Here, the situation is more complex. For the 58 names, there are many more candidate records in the census than the 58. This only means that it is not that for each case there is strictly one case reported in the census, so a possibility exists that the persons characterised by Milivoje Ivanisevic are not exactly the same persons as the one on the Srebrenica missing persons list. In order to draw my conclusions with more certainty, I need additional information about the individuals listed by Ivanisevic than my matching with the census and the ICRC list of missing will be more certain, but there is also one more interesting finding. I was trying to match the 58 names with the two mortality databases, the RS mortality database, and FIS, that is FIS mortality database with official death notifications. We discussed these databases earlier today and, as a matter of fact, court declarations that were used in the book by Milivoje Ivanisevic is this sort of document that would be accepted by statistical authority in the absence of death certificate. And honestly my expectation was that I could find the 58 names, in particular, in the RS mortality database, but it wasn't the case. So I wonder why not and what kind of court declarations are those declarations used by Mr. Ivanisevic. On the other hand, it is important to note that Mr. Ivanisevic is a very well-known activist that is engaged, and has been for years engaged, in fighting for the truth about the suffering of the Serb people during the war, especially in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He is one of the people associated with Radovan Karadzic and his Defence, and, yeah, I don't think he is 100 percent reliable source for this kind of work. He is not a statistician. He used to work in cultural planning. He is based in Belgrade, in Serbia, so he worked there. So I don't think this source is -- can be 100 percent trusted. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, were you able to find out if any of the names that are indicated, that is, of the 58 names you reviewed, were found in mass graves or identified in the ICMP data concerning those graves?

Oh, yes, it is very many of the 58, 52 have been identified by ICMP and for the 52 cases, DNA matching reports are available and site names are available and this can be provided, of course, any time. So it is quite a number, 52 out of 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We're out of time and that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. One clarification, please. You have mentioned the person, I heard the name Ivanisevic. It was recorded in different ways: Ivanisovicis, Ivanovic, can you spell the name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is Milivoje Ivanisevic. Milivoje Ivanisevic Milivoje Ivanisevic -- I will look at it. It is Milivoje, not Milivoj. The E is lacking at the first name, the last letter. Milivoje, yes. Ivanisevic, I-v-a-n-i-s-e-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. We must adjourn for the day -- Ivanisevic. Now we have it on the screen. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing about the same topic I mentioned at the beginning. Very briefly, I would like to list four documents whose translation we need as soon as possible. The 65 ter numbers are as follows. 2152, 7225, 7227, and 7224.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please look at the transcript, if these numbers are now recorded correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they are, Your Honour. I was checking it as I was reading it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sure that the Registry will forward this request to the relevant translation unit. We have to adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of March, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
